body: A woman of fifty-eight is making Sunday lunch for nine people in a kitchen that comfortably holds four, and the radio has been on since she got back from the shops. She came to this country at twenty-eight and has cooked in this kitchen for twenty-two years. A hymn starts. She knows it — she has known it since she was a child, in the version her grandmother sang, and she starts singing along without stopping what she is doing. It takes her most of the first verse to notice that she is singing different words to the ones coming out of the radio, and a slightly different tune underneath them, and that she has been putting the stress in a place the English version does not put it. She does not switch to theirs. She turns the potatoes down.

Those are not two versions of one song. They are two songs that agree about their subject. One of them is hers and one of them is a very careful account of somebody else’s, and every person who has ever sung both knows the difference in their body long before they could explain it.

40 of the stations on this band broadcast in 29 languages other than English — Spanish, Portuguese, Mandarin, Hindi, Arabic, Swahili, Yoruba, Amharic, Romanian, Korean, Tagalog, Vietnamese and more. They are not English stations with subtitles.

The word hosted is doing precise work there and is worth taking literally. A host is somebody whose house it is. They set the table before you arrived, they know where things are kept, and they are not consulting anybody about how the evening should go. A translator is a guest with excellent manners. Each of these frequencies is hosted in its own language by the persona who carries that culture, and the catalogue behind them was written in those languages rather than run through a translator afterwards — which means the songs were composed by people making decisions in that language about where a line should breathe.

Each language holds one frequency of its own, with its own host and its own bases. Jubilee Praise in Romanian is anchored in Bucharest and relayed through Sacramento and Chicago, which is where the Romanian congregations in America actually are.

None of that is the cheap way to do it, and the cheap way was available. Translating one catalogue into every language is a single body of work that scales; commissioning writers, a host and a catalogue per language is that same work done many times over, and it will never be finished. That expense is accepted deliberately, because the alternative produces something that is recognisably foreign, and a listener hearing it knows immediately that they are being reached rather than being sung to. Nobody has ever been at home in a translation of somebody else’s house.

The rest of the world has settled the other way, and settled quietly. The ordinary experience of being a non-English speaker online is an interface offered in your language and written in California — the words correct, the rhythm imported, the humour surviving as a shape where a joke used to be. It is nobody’s fault. It is what happens when localisation is a cost line rather than a purpose, and the effect is a world that has been made available to you without ever quite addressing you.

A translated worship song keeps the words and loses the music. Not the melody — the music: the phrasing, the stress, the way a line is meant to sit, the internal rhyme that carried the point and cannot survive a different vocabulary. What arrives is doctrinally sound and prosodically homeless. It can be sung. It cannot be sung the way the singer sings anything else, which is precisely the thing a worship song was supposed to unlock.
This is a claim about the mouth as much as about the heart. It is very hard to be undefended in a second language.

Be fair to translation, because it has done enormous good and this is not a case against missionaries. Translated hymns crossed oceans and taught the faith to people who had nothing else, and a translated hymn is immeasurably better than silence; whole churches were built on repertoire that arrived that way, and they were right to receive it. But those hymns were the beginning of something, not the end of it, and every one of those churches eventually started writing its own. That is the normal, healthy sequence. What is strange is a global industry two centuries later still shipping the beginning, as though the mature thing were a translated catalogue rather than a native one.
Nobody prays in their second language if their first is available.

A grandmother is staying for three months in her son’s house in a town where she knows nobody and nobody speaks her language, and the son is at work from seven until six. She is seventy-nine and has been sleeping badly and has run out of things to tidy. He has left a station on in the kitchen, low, mostly because he did not want the house to be silent when he shut the door. When he comes in that evening she is at the table with the volume where he left it and a cup of tea gone cold, and she has been singing quietly, and she does not stop when he arrives and does not explain it. He puts the kettle on. He finds, over the following weeks, that she is up before he leaves.
Nothing was translated for that woman and nothing was explained to her. A room in a country she does not speak was simply made to sound like a room she already knew how to be in.

The cost of doing it this way is fragmentation, and it is real. A dial arranged by language means a Yoruba speaker and a Korean speaker on the same band share nothing they could sing together, which is a genuine loss for a faith that claims to be one body. The international catalogues are also younger and smaller than the English ones, so a listener will hear a track come round again sooner. Building one shared repertoire in one shared language would be tidier, cheaper and easier to defend.

But that has been tried, and Scripture is unusually pointed about it. The one project in history to build a single tongue for everybody ended with the tongues multiplied, and when the Spirit came the miracle was not that everybody suddenly spoke Greek. It was that each man heard, in the language in which he was born, the wonderful works of God. The multiplicity is not the problem to be engineered away. It is the shape of the thing, chosen on purpose, and any band that flattens it for the sake of a tidier catalogue is undoing at some expense the very thing that was given.

So a believer in Bucharest or Lagos or Seoul gets a station that sounds like home, on the same dial as everyone else — not a courtesy edition, not a subtitled feed, not the English station with the words changed, but a frequency of its own with a host who lives inside the language and a catalogue written by people who were thinking in it. The dial is one dial. What is on each number was made where it is from.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there is the international stretch of the dial, one language to a frequency, which is where this article has been pointing all along.

If you want somewhere to begin, begin at HM 320.30 — Familia Inspire. It is the Spanish-language flagship, hosted by Santiago Inspire, anchored in Mexico City and relayed through Los Angeles and Miami, with Mañana Familia at eight in the morning and Familia de Noche at eight at night. If there is Spanish anywhere in your house — a parent, a neighbour, a colleague in the van, the woman who does the school run with you — put it on where they can hear it. And if there is not, put it on anyway for half an hour, because thirty minutes of a station that is plainly not translating anything for your benefit will teach you the difference this article has been describing faster than the article can.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which languages people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next frequency gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an argument about method. You are not being asked to have a view on translation, and you certainly do not need to learn a language this afternoon. Put HM 320.30 on in the kitchen the next time somebody is in your house who did not grow up speaking what you speak, and then go and do something else entirely. You will know it has worked when you come back in and they have not turned it down, and they do not explain it, and you do not ask.
